Chemotherapy-induced thrombocyto- penia can be managed with transfusion of platelets (p.1076). Recombinant thrombopoietin1 (p.1080), interleukin-3 (p.1073), and interleukin-6 have been evaluated for their abil- ity to increase platelet numbers in vivo. Interleukin-11 has also been studied and is now available as oprelvekin (p.1074), which can reduce chemotherapy-induced thrombocytope- nia.2,3 Interleukin-1 (p.2325) has also been investigated in the prevention or treatment of thrombocytopenia. The American Society of Clinical Oncology has issued guide- lines for the use of platelet transfusion.4 They recommend that prophylactic platelet transfusion be given for thrombocytopenia resulting from impaired bone-marrow function to reduce the risk of haemorrhage when the platelet count falls below a predefined threshold. This threshold will vary depending on the patient’s di- agnosis, clinical condition, and treatment modality. A threshold of 10 000 cells/mm3 has been recommended for patients being treated for acute leukaemia, with haematopoietic stem cell trans- plantation, or for solid tumours. A higher threshold of 20 000 cells/mm3 may need to be considered for patients with signs of haemorrhage, high fever, rapid fall of platelet count, coagulation abnormalities, patients receiving aggressive therapy for bladder tumours, or those with necrotic solid tumours who are at in- creased risk of bleeding from these sites. 1.
